stories.title: Snow to turbine
stories.description: How much water will reach an Alpine reservoir this summer, read from free Copernicus layers in April: catchment, snowpack, rain, soil, and the pool itself.

content.title: The catchment
content.description:
A reservoir plant's summer output is set in winter, by the snow that falls in its catchment. The reading therefore starts upstream.

The map shows the drainage basins of the eastern Alps from HydroBASINS over the river network. Thick lines mark major basins and thin lines their sub-basins. Trentino, in the centre, drains to the Adige through the Noce and the Avisio.

Each layer that follows is read inside one of these boundaries.

content.title: Snow water equivalent
content.description:
In April most of the year's inflow is still on the mountain. Snow water equivalent is the depth of water the snowpack would yield if it melted at once.

The layer shows the EFAS snow water equivalent for 15 April 2024, at the end of the snowiest Alpine winter in a decade. Pale colours mark a thin pack and dark colours a deep one.

The same product is available for every day since October 2019.

content.title: Snow anomaly
content.description:
Operators read the departure from normal before the absolute depth, because the plant's rule curve already assumes an average year.

The layer shows the ten-day snow water equivalent anomaly for 15 April 2022, in the spring before the Po ran dry, against the EFAS climatology of 1990 to 2016. White is near normal, blue and purple above normal, yellow and red below. The deficit runs across the western and southern Alps and includes the Trentino catchments.

On the same date in 2024 the map was almost entirely white and blue.

content.title: Precipitation
content.description:
Snow is the stock and rain the flow. Observed precipitation shows what has arrived in the past 24 hours.

The layer shows 1 April 2024, when an Easter storm brought heavy rain to the valleys and about a metre of snow to the peaks. Rain on a deep spring snowpack melts it and adds to it at once, and the inflow arrives within days rather than weeks.

On most days the layer is empty, because it covers the last 24 hours only.

content.title: Soil moisture anomaly
content.description:
Dry ground absorbs the melt. Saturated ground passes it to the river. The same snowpack can therefore produce very different inflows.

The layer shows the soil moisture anomaly for 15 April 2022: yellow and red almost everywhere, a dry soil under a thin snowpack. Part of what melted that spring never reached a turbine.

Two years later the same map was blue and purple in the high valleys and red on the plain to the south.

content.title: The reservoir
content.description:
The chain ends at the pool. This is Santa Giustina on the Noce, below Val di Sole, with the plants of the Noce cascade marked by capacity and type.

The shading records how often each 10 m pixel held water in 402 cloud-free Sentinel-2 passes since 2017. Dark blue is the permanent pool, water in at least nine passes out of ten. Mid blue is the drawdown zone, water in between half and nine tenths of the passes: the storage that the operator uses and the drought takes. Pale blue is occasional water at the inflow and on the northern arm.

No gauge was needed to draw it, and the same method works on any reservoir, including one upstream in another country.

content.title: Where the free data stop
content.description:
Every layer in this story is free, covers all of Europe, and is updated daily or faster: the catchment, the snowpack and its anomaly, the rain, the soil, and the reservoir extent.

None of them gives an inflow forecast in cubic metres or the water level behind a particular dam. Commercial services start there, with snow water equivalent at 20 m assimilated into a catchment model, streamflow forecasts from hours to a season ahead, and altimetry for the level.

The free layers are the screening step. They show where a paid service would pay for itself.

stories.title: The ice in the inflow
stories.description: The Adamello and Presanella glaciers feed the Sarca, the Noce, and the Oglio. What the satellites show of their retreat, and what that means for late-summer inflow.

content.title: The plants below the ice
content.description:
The Adamello and Presanella groups feed three river systems with hydropower cascades: the Sarca to the east, the Noce to the north, and the Oglio to the west.

In August, once the winter snow has gone, melt from the ice is a large part of what still reaches these plants. The map shows the plants by capacity and type, the catchment boundaries, and the glacier outlines in red.

The outlines come from the Randolph Glacier Inventory and date from 2003. The next two steps show what has happened to the ice since.

content.title: September 2018
content.description:
Sentinel-2 on 26 September 2018, at the end of the melt season and before the first snow, at 10 m. Ice is white and grey, rock is brown, and the red line is the outline of 2003.

Where rock shows inside the line, the ice has gone. The lower tongues and the margins of the plateau already sit well inside it. Surveys reported by Copernicus put the Adamello glacier at about 14 km² today, about 4 km² less than 33 years earlier, and about 65 m thinner.

content.title: September 2025
content.description:
The same view on 19 September 2025, seven years later.

The Mandrone tongue retreated 139 m in 2022 alone, against an average of about 15 m a year over the previous five years, according to the glaciological commission of the Tridentine Alpinists Society. The surveys reported by Copernicus give a thinning of 5.9 m in 2021 and about 4.5 m a year on average.

Sentinel-2 gives the extent every year, free, for every glacier in the Alps. The thickness, which is what inflow depends on, comes from elevation models, altimetry, and field measurement.

content.title: What it means for inflow
content.description:
A shrinking glacier first gives more water, then less. Melt rises while the ice thins and falls once the ice is gone. For most Alpine basins the rise is over.

Swiss glaciers lost a tenth of their volume in 2022 and 2023 together and a further 2.5 per cent in 2024, according to GLAMOS. The Italian side has no equivalent network, which is one reason the satellite record matters here.

For the plants on the Sarca, the Noce, and the Oglio, the late-summer inflow that the ice guaranteed is becoming an inflow that the weather decides.

content.title: The resource that does not come back
content.description:
The 2003 inventory holds 1,815 Alpine glaciers of 0.1 km² or more, 2,036 km² of ice, almost all of it above the reservoirs that make the Alps the storage battery of the European grid.

Snow returns each winter. Ice does not. The hydropower system was built on both, and the second is being withdrawn within the lifetime of the plants on this map.

stories.title: Solar arrays in Puglia
stories.description: Ground-mounted solar arrays detected in Sentinel-2 imagery around Troia, Puglia, with the solar resource, land cover, and the transmission grid.

content.title: Solar resource
content.description:
Southern Italy receives some of the highest surface solar radiation in Europe. The layer shows all-sky downward shortwave radiation at the surface for June 2021 from NASA CERES, on a one-degree grid of about 80 km.

At this resolution the map shows only the regional gradient. Site assessments use finer satellite-derived irradiance data.

content.title: Aerosols
content.description:
Aerosols reduce the radiation that reaches a panel, most of all on clear summer days. The layer shows MODIS aerosol optical depth for 15 August 2024. That day the highest values lay over the Pannonian basin, the Balkans, and North Africa. Southern Italy was comparatively clear.

Daily aerosol and cloud data explain much of the week-to-week variation in a plant's output.

content.title: Troia
content.description:
Troia lies south-west of Foggia, in farmland at the foot of the Monti Dauni. The province of Foggia is one of Italy's main areas for wind and solar development.

The base map is a cloud-free Sentinel-2 mosaic at 10 m. Solar arrays are present but hard to tell apart from the surrounding fields.

content.title: Detected arrays
content.description:
EURAC Research detected 252 ground-mounted solar arrays in this area in Sentinel-2 imagery from 2025, with a method run on the ESA APEx platform. Together they cover about 218 ha.

Most are small. The median array covers about a third of a hectare and the largest about 11 ha. A register limited to large plants would miss most of them.

content.title: Land cover
content.description:
CORINE Land Cover 2018 classifies almost the whole area as non-irrigated arable land, mostly durum wheat in this part of Puglia. Nearly all detected arrays stand on it.

Solar on farmland is contested in Italian energy policy. Repeating the detection each year would show how much farmland is converted.

content.title: Grid
content.description:
Two 380 kV lines pass within a few kilometres of the arrays. In southern Italy, requests to connect new solar and wind far exceed what the network can take, so grid capacity is one of the main limits on new projects.

The layer shows line routes and voltages. Spare capacity at each substation comes from the grid operator.

content.title: Uses and limits
content.description:
Satellite detection gives the location and footprint of every array, registered or not. Planners, grid operators, statistics offices, and insurers can all use it.

It does not give installed capacity, panel type, or output. Those come from registers, very high resolution imagery, and operators.

stories.title: Solar and wind in Austria
stories.description: Solar and wind potential across Austria from the ESA GTIF Austria demonstrator, with land cover and the transmission grid.

content.title: Solar potential
content.description:
Solar potential varies little across Austria. The layer shows annual solar power potential from the ESA GTIF Austria demonstrator, modelled by DHI from irradiance, temperature, and terrain, and resampled here from 13 m to 100 m. The colour scale runs from 2.8 to 3.7 kWh/m² a day to bring out the differences.

The highest values lie in the east and south-east and on high south-facing slopes. The lowest lie in Alpine valleys and on north-facing slopes.

content.title: Wind potential
content.description:
Wind varies far more. Wind power density at 100 m, also from GTIF, ranges from about 50 W/m² in sheltered basins to more than 1,500 W/m² on Alpine crests.

The crests are largely unbuildable. In the lowlands the resource is highest in the north-east. The colour scale stops at 800 W/m² so that differences in the lowlands remain visible.

content.title: The north-east
content.description:
On the Parndorf plateau and in the Weinviertel, east and north of Vienna, wind power density at 100 m reaches 380 to 450 W/m². The Graz and Klagenfurt basins reach 50 to 120.

Most Austrian wind farms stand in Lower Austria and Burgenland, close to the 220 kV and 380 kV lines that supply Vienna.

content.title: Constraints
content.description:
Land use determines where a project can be permitted. CORINE Land Cover 2018 shows Vienna and surrounding towns in red, forest in green, farmland in yellow, and Lake Neusiedl, a national park and UNESCO site, to the south.

Settlement buffers, forest, and protected areas narrow the area in which a good resource can be used.

content.title: GTIF Austria
content.description:
GTIF Austria combines resource, land, and grid data for one country at a resolution useful to municipalities. ESA has since applied the approach to other countries and regions.

The full Austrian layer set is open at gtif.esa.int.

stories.title: Offshore wind and wakes in the North Sea
stories.description: Wind, depth, and waves in the North Sea, the wind farms of the German Bight, and two Sentinel-1 scenes of wakes crossing between Dutch and German farms.

content.title: Wind
content.description:
Offshore wind farms cluster in the southern North Sea, where winds are strong, water shallow, and ports close. The layer shows mean wind speed 10 m above the sea for January 2025 from the Copernicus Marine wind product, which combines satellite scatterometer data with reanalysis. Darker green means stronger wind.

The outlines are wind farms from EMODnet: yellow in operation, blue under construction or approved, grey planned.

content.title: Depth
content.description:
Water depth determines the foundation. Fixed foundations are standard to about 50 m. Deeper sites need floating turbines, which remain more expensive.

EMODnet bathymetry shows why the southern North Sea was built first. The Dogger Bank and the German Bight are shallow, while the Norwegian Trench is several hundred metres deep. Several planned zones lie in deeper water further offshore.

content.title: Waves
content.description:
Waves determine foundation loads and the days on which crews can reach turbines. The layer shows significant wave height from the Copernicus Marine wave analysis at 06:00 UTC on 24 January 2025, as Storm Éowyn crossed Ireland and Scotland. The storm left about a million people without power.

The highest waves lay west of Ireland. The North Sea, sheltered by Britain, saw much lower waves. The same product forecasts waves 10 days ahead.

content.title: German Bight
content.description:
North of the East Frisian islands, Dutch and German farms stand close together. The southern row runs from Gemini on the Dutch side to Borkum Riffgrund, Trianel Windpark Borkum, Merkur, and Gode Wind on the German side. Global Tech I, Hohe See, Albatros, and BARD Offshore 1 stand further north.

Each farm is permitted separately, but each affects the wind that reaches its neighbours.

content.title: Wakes, westerly wind
content.description:
Sentinel-1 radar measures sea-surface roughness. Wind-roughened water appears bright, calmer water dark, and turbines as bright points. On 19 September 2024 the wind blew from the west.

Dark wakes extend east of the farms for tens of kilometres and reach the farms downwind. Turbines inside a wake produce less power.

content.title: Wakes, easterly wind
content.description:
On 25 December 2025 the wind blew from the east. The wakes run west, from the German farms across the border towards Gemini.

Wake losses between neighbouring farms are a growing issue in North Sea planning. Sentinel-1 covers the area every few days at no cost. Converting the images into wind-speed deficits requires processing that commercial providers offer.

content.title: Interconnectors
content.description:
High-voltage direct-current cables already cross the North Sea, including NorNed between Norway and the Netherlands, NordLink between Norway and Germany, and Viking Link between Denmark and Britain.

Future farms further offshore will connect through hubs shared by several countries. Planning them requires the wind, depth, wave, wake, and grid data shown in this story.

stories.title: Wildfire and the grid in north-west Iberia
stories.description: Wildfire exposure of the transmission grid in north-west Iberia, from long-term fire frequency to the August 2025 fires and the areas they burnt.

content.title: Fire frequency
content.description:
North-west Iberia has one of the densest concentrations of repeatedly burnt land in western Europe. The layer, from the Global Wildfire Information System, counts how often MODIS has mapped each location as burnt since 2000. Darker colours mean more frequent fires.

Galicia, northern Portugal, and the mountains of León and Zamora stand out.

content.title: Transmission lines
content.description:
Several 400 kV (red) and 220 kV (orange) lines run from Galicia and the Sil valley towards central Spain through frequently burnt areas.

Fire near a line can force the operator to switch it off, because smoke and heat make the air conductive. Fire that reaches a pylon can bring the line down.

content.title: Active fires, 11 to 18 August 2025
content.description:
Between 11 and 18 August 2025, large fires burnt across Ourense, León, Zamora, and northern Portugal. By 21 August EFFIS estimated that more than 380,000 ha had burnt in Spain in 2025, the worst season since 1994.

The blocks show every location flagged by the Meteosat active-fire product in at least one of 96 two-hourly images that week, red for fire and amber for potential fire. Each Meteosat pixel covers about 4 km by 5 km here.

content.title: Burnt areas, 2025
content.description:
EFFIS mapped every burnt area of 30 ha or more in 2025 from MODIS and Sentinel-2. The largest lie in eastern Ourense, around A Rúa and Larouco, and in León and Zamora.

Measured on this map, roughly 330 km of 220 kV and 400 kV line in north-west Iberia crossed land that burnt in 2025. The figure is approximate, given the map resolution.

content.title: Sil valley
content.description:
Eastern Ourense around the Sil valley, on a Sentinel-2 mosaic from 2024, before the fires. A 400 kV line and several 220 kV lines cross areas that burnt in August 2025.

At this scale the map identifies the spans that crossed burnt ground and the stretches where unburnt vegetation remains close to the line.

content.title: Summary
content.description:
The three layers serve different stages. Fire frequency supports line routing and vegetation management, Meteosat detection supports operations during a fire, and burnt-area maps support inspection afterwards.

All three are free and cover Europe. The condition of individual pylons, or of vegetation along a span, requires very high resolution imagery, lidar, or drone surveys. The live active-fire layer is in the Infrastructure group.

stories.title: Fossil fuel emissions from Sentinel-5P
stories.description: Sentinel-5P annual averages of nitrogen dioxide over large lignite plants and of methane over oil and gas regions, with the import rules of the EU Methane Regulation.

content.title: Nitrogen dioxide, 2025
content.description:
Sentinel-5P measures nitrogen dioxide, a product of combustion, daily across the globe. The layer shows the 2025 average on a grid of about 2.5 km.

The highest values lie over the Po valley, the Benelux and Rhine-Ruhr, Paris, London, and Madrid, driven mainly by traffic and industry. Most power plants are hard to separate from nearby cities.

content.title: Bełchatów
content.description:
Bełchatów, in central Poland, is Europe's largest lignite power plant at about 5 GW. It has topped rankings of the EU's largest carbon dioxide emitters for years and is due to close by 2036.

In the 2025 average the nitrogen dioxide column over the plant (green ring) is higher than over Łódź (white ring), a city of about 650,000 people 50 km to the north.

content.title: Rhineland
content.description:
RWE's Neurath and Niederaussem plants, west of Cologne, burn lignite from the Rhineland mines. RWE closed five units there, 2.1 GW in total, on 31 March 2024 and plans to end coal use by 2030.

In the 2025 average the plants read only slightly higher than Cologne. At this resolution their signal merges with the traffic and industry of the Rhine-Ruhr.

content.title: Obrenovac
content.description:
The Nikola Tesla A and B plants at Obrenovac, on the Sava about 30 km from Belgrade, burn Kolubara lignite. With about 2.9 GW they supply almost half of Serbia's electricity.

In the 2025 average the column over the plant is higher than over Belgrade.

content.title: Methane, 2025
content.description:
Sentinel-5P also measures methane, at about 5 km. Leaks from wells, pipelines, and compressors make oil and gas one of the largest human sources.

In the 2025 average, western Turkmenistan stands out clearly. Elsewhere, rice, livestock, and wetlands raise values over large areas. Stripes over the sea and gaps over mountains and snow are retrieval artefacts.

content.title: Permian Basin
content.description:
The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico is the largest US oil field. Its gas supplies US LNG export terminals, now Europe's largest source of LNG. Aircraft and satellite surveys have found some of the world's largest methane leaks there.

In the 2025 average the basin barely stands out. Large leaks are intermittent, and annual averaging at 5 km removes them. Detecting individual leaks requires dedicated plume-mapping satellites.

content.title: EU Methane Regulation
content.description:
The EU Methane Regulation of 2024 applies to imports. From 1 January 2027, importers of oil, gas, and coal must show that their suppliers monitor and verify methane emissions to EU-equivalent standards. From August 2028 they must report the methane intensity of their supplies, and from 2030 meet maximum values.

In July 2026 the Commission recommended that member states not fine importers for 2027 to 2029. The obligations still apply. Satellite data offers an independent check on supplier claims.
